The queen check on d2 is forcing because the white king has no legal flight squares (all adjacent squares are either occupied, on the check line, or attacked by the queen or Black's f5-pawn) and cannot capture on d2 (protected by the knight on c4). The only legal reply is therefore the bishop capture on d2.

After the forced capture the knight delivers the second check from e5. The d6-pawn is absolutely pinned to the king by the d7-rook, so it cannot capture the knight. All remaining king flights are covered by Black's remaining pieces or are still under attack, and no interposition is possible. The result is forced mate on the second move.

In either case the reply h5xg6 is mate: the capture vacates h5 and thereby opens a discovered rook check along the h-file while simultaneously removing the capturer. The three-ply line therefore forces mate in two moves irrespective of Black’s choice of recapture.

This capture deflects the queen away from its defensive post on the d-file. With the knight no longer blocking the e-file, the follow-up Re7xe3+ simultaneously checks the king on f3 and attacks the now-undefended knight on d3. Because the queen has been deflected, White cannot recapture on d3 after the king moves out of check, so Black nets a full piece. The three-ply sequence is therefore forced in the main line and directly realizes the fork.

The key tactical idea is a queen fork of the white king and rook, made possible by first clearing the c5–b4 diagonal. Black begins with the pawn capture c5xd4. If White recaptures with the only natural reply c3xd4, the c-file pawn disappears and the diagonal opens. Black then swings the queen d6–b4.  

From b4 the queen delivers check along the now-clear diagonal (path c3 empty) while simultaneously attacking the undefended rook on h4 along the fourth rank. The square b4 cannot be captured by any white unit: the king, queen, rooks, bishop and knight all lack a safe attacking line to it. White must therefore resolve the check, after which Black simply collects the rook with Qxh4, emerging a full exchange ahead.  

All alternative recaptures after the initial c5xd4 allow the same Qb4 idea or even stronger continuations, confirming that the three-ply sequence is forcing and decisive.

The position features a classic pin opportunity on the diagonal linking White's king (e2) and rook (f3). Black begins by playing Be6-g4; the bishop is safe because no White unit attacks g4, and the move places the rook under an absolute pin (any departure of the rook would illegally expose the king to check).

The most challenging of these is the counter-attacking b4-b5, which threatens the black rook on c6. Black ignores the threat and simply executes the pin by capturing the immobilized rook (Bg4xf3). The resulting material gain (rook for bishop) is decisive; any subsequent recapture by White's king still leaves Black ahead by two points while the c6-rook can step out of danger on the next move. This three-ply sequence therefore constitutes the main line of the pin tactic.

The key tactic exploits an under-protected piece combined with removal of its sole defender. Black’s knight on e4 captures the undefended bishop on g3 (e4g3). This bishop is White’s only guard of the advanced knight on g6. White’s most natural recapture is with the queen (f3g3). With the bishop gone, that knight is now entirely undefended, allowing Black’s f7-pawn to capture it safely (f7g6). The three-ply sequence therefore nets a full piece: Black gains the bishop, returns the knight, then regains the second knight. Any alternative White recapture on g3 leaves the same undefended knight for Black to harvest on the next move.
